L1: name: winui-setup
L2: description: "Install and verify WinUI 3 prerequisites — .NET SDK 8.0.100+, WinApp CLI 0.7+, and Developer Mode; identify additional Native AOT and Windows Sandbox requirements. Use when the user asks to set up or repair the toolchain, or when another WinUI skill finds a missing or outdated prerequisite."
L3: ---
L4: ### Purpose
L5: 
L6: Install and verify the prerequisites every other `winui-*` skill assumes. WinApp CLI 0.7 owns WinUI template discovery and installation through `winapp new`; **do not install the template pack separately**. The project's target framework may require a newer .NET SDK than the CLI's minimum.
L7: > [!IMPORTANT]
L8: > Install per-user prerequisites (WinApp CLI) without asking, and tell the user what changed. **Ask before anything that needs admin rights (UAC) or a large toolchain** — the .NET SDK, Developer Mode, and Native AOT build tools. Windows Sandbox enablement is the user's to do.
L9: 
L10: This skill is idempotent: detect everything first, install or upgrade only what is needed, and print one final summary.
L11: ### Steps
L12: 
L13: #### Detect everything
L14: 
L15: Run these checks together so the user sees the full state before anything changes:
L16: 
L17: ```powershell
L18: $minimumDotNet = [version]'8.0.100'
L19: $minimumWinApp = [version]'0.7.0'
L20: # .NET SDK — project-mode winapp run requires SDK 8.0.100+
L21: $dotnetSdks = @(& dotnet --list-sdks 2>$null) | ForEach-Object {
L22:     $text = ($_ -replace ' \[.*$','').Trim()
L23:     $parsed = $null
L24:     if ([version]::TryParse(($text -split '-')[0], [ref]$parsed)) { $parsed }
L25: }
L26: $dotnetVersion = $dotnetSdks |
L27:     Where-Object { $_ -ge $minimumDotNet } |
L28:     Sort-Object -Descending |
L29:     Select-Object -First 1
L30: $dotnetOk = $null -ne $dotnetVersion
L31: # WinApp CLI — require released 0.7+ for the migrated workflows
L32: $winappCmd = Get-Command winapp -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
L33: $winappVersion = $null
L34: $winappPrerelease = $false
L35: if ($winappCmd) {
L36:     foreach ($line in @(& winapp --version 2>$null)) {
L37:         $match = [regex]::Match(
L38:             [string]$line,
L39:             '^\s*v?(?<version>\d+\.\d+\.\d+)(?:-(?<prerelease>[0-9A-Za-z.-]+))?(?:\+[0-9A-Za-z.-]+)?\s*$'
L40:         )
L41:         if ($match.Success) {
L42:             $parsed = $null
L43:             if ([version]::TryParse($match.Groups['version'].Value, [ref]$parsed)) {
L44:                 $winappVersion = $parsed
L45:                 $winappPrerelease = $match.Groups['prerelease'].Success
L46:             }
L47:         }
L48:     }
L49: }
L50: $winappOk = ($winappVersion -ge $minimumWinApp) -and -not $winappPrerelease
L51: # Developer Mode
L52: $devModeOk = ((Get-ItemProperty `
L53:     -Path 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\AppModelUnlock' `
L54:     -Name AllowDevelopmentWithoutDevLicense -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
L55: ).AllowDevelopmentWithoutDevLicense) -eq 1
L56: ```
L57: 
L58: Print a one-shot status table:
L59: 
L60: ```text
L61: .NET SDK >= 8.0.100     [OK] found 10.0.100
L62: WinApp CLI >= 0.7.0     [!] found 0.6.0 — will upgrade
L63: Developer Mode          [X] disabled — needs admin to enable
L64: ```
L65: 
L66: #### Install what's missing
L67: ##### .NET SDK (ask first)
L68: 
L69: The SDK installer is machine-wide and triggers UAC. **Ask the user first.** When they agree and no SDK at or above `8.0.100` was found, install the recommended SDK:
L70: 
L71: ```powershell
L72: winget install --id Microsoft.DotNet.SDK.10 --exact --silent --accept-package-agreements --accept-source-agreements
L73: ```
L74: Do not install another SDK when one already satisfies both the CLI minimum and
L75: the requested project's target framework / `global.json`. The CLI's minimum
L76: does not let an 8.x SDK build a `net10.0-windows` app.
L77: If the base check passed but the requested project needs another SDK, report
L78: that requirement and offer to install its matching SDK rather than declaring
L79: the project ready. If the user declines, print the command for later use.
L80: ##### WinApp CLI (no admin needed)
L81: 
L82: WinApp CLI is a per-user MSIX package, so install or upgrade it **without asking** and tell the user what changed. If `winapp` is missing, install it. If it is below released 0.7.0, upgrade it. Skip both when the installed version already meets the minimum:
L83: 
L84: ```powershell
L85: # When winapp is missing
L86: winget install --id Microsoft.WinAppCli --exact --silent --accept-package-agreements --accept-source-agreements
L87: # When winapp does not meet the released 0.7.0 minimum
L88: winget upgrade --id Microsoft.WinAppCli --exact --silent --accept-package-agreements --accept-source-agreements
L89: ```
L90: 
L91: Refresh PATH after any winget install or upgrade:
L92: 
L93: ```powershell
L94: $env:Path = [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable('Path','Machine') + ';' +
L95:             [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable('Path','User')
L96: ```
L97: Run the version detection again. If a released `0.7.0` or later is still unavailable, report the actual version and mark setup blocked; do not fall back to older commands. A prerelease doesn't meet the requirement unless the user asks for preview validation.
L98: ##### Developer Mode (ask first)
L99: 
L100: Developer Mode requires admin elevation. **Ask the user before triggering UAC.** Only if they agree, elevate this one operation:
L101: ```powershell
L102: Start-Process powershell -Verb RunAs -ArgumentList @(
L103:     '-NoProfile','-Command',
L104:     "New-Item -Path 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\AppModelUnlock' -Force | Out-Null; " +
L105:     "Set-ItemProperty -Path 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\AppModelUnlock' " +
L106:     "-Name AllowDevelopmentWithoutDevLicense -Type DWord -Value 1"
L107: ) -Wait
L108: ```
L109: 
L110: If the user declines or dismisses UAC, continue to the summary and print the command for later use.
L111: #### Additional requirements for the requested workflow
L112: | Workflow | Additional requirements |
L113: |---|---|
L114: | Native AOT publish/run | Windows native compiler/linker toolchain: Visual Studio or Build Tools with **Desktop development with C++**, including the target architecture's tools and Windows SDK. See [Native AOT prerequisites](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/core/deploying/native-aot/). These are not required for normal JIT iteration. |
L115: | Windows Sandbox app runs and UI automation (preferred when available) | WinApp's integration requires Windows 11 24H2+, hardware virtualization, and a working Windows Sandbox feature/client. Supported editions include **Pro, Enterprise, and Education; not Home**. Input/capture needs an unlocked host and a connected, non-minimized client. See [WinApp Sandbox prerequisites](https://github.com/microsoft/winappCli/blob/main/docs/sandbox-execution.md#prerequisites). |
L116: Report these separately from the base toolchain. `winapp target snapshot sandbox --json` inspects an existing
L117: guest without starting or repairing it; "no target running" alone does not
L118: mean the Windows feature is unavailable. `winui-ui-testing`
L119: Step 1 defines what to do when Windows Sandbox is unavailable.
L120: Enabling Windows Sandbox is a **user action** (admin plus a reboot): ask the user
L121: to open **Turn Windows features on or off**, select **Windows Sandbox**, and
L122: restart if prompted. Hardware virtualization must be enabled; a VM may also
L123: require nested virtualization. See Microsoft's
L124: [supported editions](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/security/application-security/application-isolation/windows-sandbox/)
L125: and [installation steps](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/security/application-security/application-isolation/windows-sandbox/windows-sandbox-install).

L1: title: Build, Run, and Launch Verification
L2: priority: CRITICAL
L3: tags: build, run, launch, verification, packaged, unpackaged, debugging
L4: sources:
L5:   - https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/apps/get-started/start-here
L6:   - https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/apps/windows-app-sdk/deploy-packaged-apps
L7:   - https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/apps/windows-app-sdk/deploy-unpackaged-apps
L8: ---
L9: ## What This Reference Is For
L10: 
L11: Use this file when the task involves building, running, launch failures, startup crashes, or final verification that a WinUI app actually opens on the current machine.
L12: ## Required Workflow
L13: 1. Identify the real build target:
L14:    - solution or project file
L15:    - configuration
L16:    - platform
L17:    - packaged or unpackaged model
L18: 2. Build after each meaningful code edit and again at task completion.
L19: 3. Run the app after changes when feasible. Always do it when the user asked for it or when startup, navigation, resources, or packaging changed.
L20: 4. Use the launch path that matches the deployment model:
L21:    - packaged local dev: normally Visual Studio deploy or another package-aware flow
L22:    - unpackaged local dev: normally the built executable the user will actually run
L23: 5. Verify real launch with objective evidence such as:
L24:    - non-zero main window handle
L25:    - expected window title
L26:    - responsive process with visible shell
L27:    - no immediate startup exception or crash
L28: 6. After completing app work, including a first scaffold or a later build-and-fix cycle, leave a successfully verified final app instance running so the user can see that it worked unless they explicitly asked you not to.
L29: 7. If launch fails or verification is ambiguous, debug the failure before saying the app is ready.
L30: ## Packaged vs Unpackaged Rules
L31: 
L32: - Choose one model intentionally before wiring startup, persistence, and launch instructions.
L33: - Packaged apps can rely on package identity and package-backed storage.
L34: - Unpackaged apps must not assume package identity. Guard or replace APIs that require it.
L35: - APIs such as `Windows.Storage.ApplicationData.Current` can fail in unpackaged runs even when the build succeeds.
L36: - Do not mix packaged-only assumptions into an unpackaged startup path.
L37: ## Build and Launch Guidance
L38: - Prefer explicit platform targets when WinUI output is sensitive to architecture defaults. If `AnyCPU` creates ambiguity, use `x64` for local verification.
L39: - For unpackaged verification, prefer launching the built `.exe` from `bin\Debug\...\win-x64\` or the project-specific output path.
L40: - After a successful final launch verification, do not immediately tear the app down just because verification succeeded; keep it open for the user unless it blocks the next required action.
L41: - If `dotnet run` throws bootstrapper, deployment, or COM activation errors, treat that as a signal that the chosen launch path or packaging setup is wrong for the current app.
L42: - Stop old app instances before rebuilding if they can lock output files.
L43: ## Debugging Startup Failures
L44: - Separate environment problems from app-code startup crashes.
L45: - If the app exits before showing a window, inspect the startup path first:
L46:   - `App.xaml`
L47:   - merged resource dictionaries
L48:   - converters
L49:   - `MainWindow`
L50:   - services used during startup
L51: - For startup or manifest issues, compare the current app against a fresh `dotnet new winui` scaffold for the same packaging model before broader surgery.
L52: - For opaque `MSB3073` and `XamlCompiler.exe` failures, simplify back toward the template-generated startup and shared-resource shape before making further structural changes.
L53: - Restore complex startup pieces incrementally when the failure point is unclear. A minimal `App.xaml` plus minimal `MainWindow` is a valid isolation step.
L54: - If the diagnostics look stale or inconsistent with the current files, run a clean build once before deeper surgery.
L55: - Prefer restoring the last known-good template-based shared-resource state over moving styles inline as the long-term fix.
L56: - When using unpackaged startup, review persistence, notifications, storage, and activation code for hidden package-identity assumptions.
L57: ## Exit Criteria
L58: 
L59: - Build succeeds from the intended local workflow.
L60: - The app launches from the intended local workflow.
L61: - A real top-level window or equivalent expected UI is confirmed.
L62: - No unresolved startup exception remains.

L5: # Preparing a new repository【1†】
L6: 
L7: The place where your backups will be saved is called a “repository”. This is simply a directory containing a set of subdirectories and files created by restic to store your backups, some corresponding metadata and encryption keys.
L8: 
L9: To access the repository, a password (also called a key) must be specified. A repository can hold multiple keys that can all be used to access the repository.
L10: This chapter explains how to create (“init”) such a repository. The repository can be stored locally, or on some remote server or service. This chapter first covers using a local repository; the remaining sections cover all the other options. You can skip to the next chapter once you’ve read the relevant section here.
L11: For automated backups, restic supports specifying the repository location in the environment variable `RESTIC_REPOSITORY`. Restic can also read the repository location from a file specified via the `--repository-file` option or the environment variable `RESTIC_REPOSITORY_FILE`.
L12: 
L13: For automating the supply of the repository password to restic, several options exist:
L14: 
L15:   * Setting the environment variable `RESTIC_PASSWORD`
L16:   * Specifying the path to a file with the password via the option `--password-file` or the environment variable `RESTIC_PASSWORD_FILE`
L17: 
L18:   * Configuring a program to be called when the password is needed via the option `--password-command` or the environment variable `RESTIC_PASSWORD_COMMAND`
L19: The `init` command has an option called `--repository-version` which can be used to explicitly set the version of the new repository. By default, the current stable version is used (see table below). The alias `latest` will always resolve to the latest repository version. Have a look at the 【2†design documentation†github.com】 for more details.
L20: 
L21: The below table shows which restic version is required to use a certain repository version, as well as notable features introduced in the various versions.
L22: Repository version  | Required restic version  | Major new features  | Comment
L23: --- | --- | --- | ---
L24: `1`  | Any  |  |
L25: `2`  | 0.14.0 or newer  | Compression support  | Current default
L26: ## Local【3†】
L27: 
L28: In order to create a repository at `/srv/restic-repo`, run the following command and enter the same password twice:
L29: 
L30:     $ restic init --repo /srv/restic-repo
L31:     enter password for new repository:
L32:     enter password again:
L33:     created restic repository 085b3c76b9 at /srv/restic-repo
L34:     Please note that knowledge of your password is required to access the repository.
L35:     Losing your password means that your data is irrecoverably lost.
L36: 
L37: 
L38: Warning
L39: Remembering your password is important! If you lose it, you won’t be able to access data stored in the repository.
L40: 
L41: Warning
L42: 
L43: On Linux, storing the backup repository on a CIFS (SMB) share or backing up data from a CIFS share is not recommended due to compatibility issues in older Linux kernels. Either use another backend or set the environment variable `GODEBUG` to `asyncpreemptoff=1`. Refer to GitHub issue 【4†#2659†github.com】 for further explanations.
L44: ## SFTP【5†】
L45: 
L46: In order to backup data via SFTP, you must first set up a server with SSH and let it know your public key. Passwordless login is important since automatic backups are not possible if the server prompts for credentials.
L47: Once the server is configured, the setup of the SFTP repository can simply be achieved by changing the URL scheme in the `init` command:
L48: 
L49:     $ restic -r sftp:user@host:/srv/restic-repo init
L50:     enter password for new repository:
L51:     enter password again:
L52:     created restic repository f1c6108821 at sftp:user@host:/srv/restic-repo
L53:     Please note that knowledge of your password is required to access the repository.
L54:     Losing your password means that your data is irrecoverably lost.
L55: You can also specify a relative (read: no slash (`/`) character at the beginning) directory, in this case the dir is relative to the remote user’s home directory.
L56: 
L57: Also, if the SFTP server is enforcing domain-confined users, you can specify the user this way: `user@domain@host`.
L58: 
L59: Note
L60: Please be aware that SFTP servers do not expand the tilde character (`~`) normally used as an alias for a user’s home directory. If you want to specify a path relative to the user’s home directory, pass a relative path to the SFTP backend.
L61: 
L62: If you need to specify a port number or IPv6 address, you’ll need to use URL syntax. E.g., the repository `/srv/restic-repo` on `[::1]` (localhost) at port 2222 with username `user` can be specified as
L63: 
L64:     sftp://user@[::1]:2222//srv/restic-repo
L65: Note the double slash: the first slash separates the connection settings from the path, while the second is the start of the path. To specify a relative path, use one slash.
L66: 
L67: Alternatively, you can create an entry in the `ssh` configuration file, usually located in your home directory at `~/.ssh/config` or in `/etc/ssh/ssh_config`:
L68: 
L69:     Host foo
L70:         User bar
L71:         Port 2222
L72: Then use the specified host name `foo` normally (you don’t need to specify the user name in this case):
L73: 
L74:     $ restic -r sftp:foo:/srv/restic-repo init
L75: 
L76: 
L77: You can also add an entry with a special host name which does not exist, just for use with restic, and use the `Hostname` option to set the real host name:
L78: 
L79:     Host restic-backup-host
L80:         Hostname foo
L81:         User bar
L82:         Port 2222
L83: Then use it in the backend specification:
L84: 
L85:     $ restic -r sftp:restic-backup-host:/srv/restic-repo init
L86: 
L87: 
L88: Last, if you’d like to use an entirely different program to create the SFTP connection, you can specify the command to be run with the option `-o sftp.command="foobar"`. Alternatively, `-o sftp.args` allows setting the arguments passed to the default SSH command (ignored when `sftp.command` is set)
L89: 
L90: Note
L91: Please be aware that SFTP servers close connections when no data is received by the client. This can happen when restic is processing huge amounts of unchanged data. To avoid this issue add the following lines to the client’s .ssh/config file:
L92: 
L93:     ServerAliveInterval 60
L94:     ServerAliveCountMax 240
L95: ## REST Server【6†】
L96: 
L97: In order to backup data to the remote server via HTTP or HTTPS protocol, you must first set up a remote 【7†REST server†github.com】 instance. Once the server is configured, accessing it is achieved by changing the URL scheme like this:
L98: 
L99:     $ restic -r rest:http://host:8000/ init
L100: Depending on your REST server setup, you can use HTTPS protocol, unix socket, password protection, multiple repositories or any combination of those features. The TCP/IP port is also configurable. Here are some more examples:
L101: 
L102:     $ restic -r rest:https://host:8000/ init
L103:     $ restic -r rest:https://user:pass@host:8000/ init
L104:     $ restic -r rest:https://user:pass@host:8000/my_backup_repo/ init
L105:     $ restic -r rest:http+unix:///tmp/rest.socket:/my_backup_repo/ init
L106: The server username and password can be specified using environment variables as well:
L107: 
L108:     $ export RESTIC_REST_USERNAME=<MY_REST_SERVER_USERNAME>
L109:     $ export RESTIC_REST_PASSWORD=<MY_REST_SERVER_PASSWORD>

L5: # Removing backup snapshots【1†】
L6: All backup space is finite, so restic allows removing old snapshots. This can be done either manually (by specifying a snapshot ID to remove) or by using a policy that describes which snapshots to forget. For all remove operations, two commands need to be called in sequence: `forget` to remove snapshots, and `prune` to remove the remaining data that was referenced only by the removed snapshots.
L7: The latter can be automated with the `--prune` option of `forget`, which runs `prune` automatically if any snapshots were actually removed.
L8: Pruning snapshots can be a time-consuming process, depending on the number of snapshots and data to process. During a prune operation, the repository is locked and backups cannot be completed. Please plan your pruning so that there’s time to complete it and it doesn’t interfere with regular backup runs.
L9: 
L10: It is advisable to run `restic check` after pruning, to make sure you are alerted, should the internal data structures of the repository be damaged.
L11: ## Removing a single snapshot【2†】
L12: The command `snapshots` can be used to list all snapshots in a repository like this:
L13: 
L14:     $ restic -r /srv/restic-repo snapshots
L15:     enter password for repository:
L16:     ID        Date                 Host      Tags  Directory
L17:     ----------------------------------------------------------------------
L18:     40dc1520  2015-05-08 21:38:30  kasimir         /home/user/work
L19:     79766175  2015-05-08 21:40:19  kasimir         /home/user/work
L20:     bdbd3439  2015-05-08 21:45:17  luigi           /home/art
L21:     590c8fc8  2015-05-08 21:47:38  kazik           /srv
L22:     9f0bc19e  2015-05-08 21:46:11  luigi           /srv
L23: In order to remove the snapshot of `/home/art`, use the `forget` command and specify the snapshot ID on the command line:
L24: 
L25:     $ restic -r /srv/restic-repo forget bdbd3439
L26:     enter password for repository:
L27:     removed snapshot bdbd3439
L28: Afterwards this snapshot is removed:
L29: 
L30:     $ restic -r /srv/restic-repo snapshots
L31:     enter password for repository:
L32:     ID        Date                 Host     Tags  Directory
L33:     ----------------------------------------------------------------------
L34:     40dc1520  2015-05-08 21:38:30  kasimir        /home/user/work
L35:     79766175  2015-05-08 21:40:19  kasimir        /home/user/work
L36:     590c8fc8  2015-05-08 21:47:38  kazik          /srv
L37:     9f0bc19e  2015-05-08 21:46:11  luigi          /srv
L38: But the data that was referenced by files in this snapshot is still stored in the repository. To cleanup unreferenced data, the `prune` command must be run:
L39: 
L40:     $ restic -r /srv/restic-repo prune
L41:     enter password for repository:
L42:     repository 33002c5e opened successfully
L43:     loading all snapshots...
L44:     loading indexes...
L45:     finding data that is still in use for 4 snapshots
L46:     [0:00] 100.00%  4 / 4 snapshots
L47:     searching used packs...
L48:     collecting packs for deletion and repacking
L49:     [0:00] 100.00%  5 / 5 packs processed
L50: 
L51:     to repack:            69 blobs / 1.078 MiB
L52:     this removes:         67 blobs / 1.047 MiB
L53:     to delete:             7 blobs / 25.726 KiB
L54:     total prune:          74 blobs / 1.072 MiB
L55:     remaining:            16 blobs / 38.003 KiB
L56:     unused size after prune: 0 B (0.00% of remaining size)
L57: 
L58:     repacking packs
L59:     [0:00] 100.00%  2 / 2 packs repacked
L60:     rebuilding index
L61:     [0:00] 100.00%  3 / 3 packs processed
L62:     deleting obsolete index files
L63:     [0:00] 100.00%  3 / 3 files deleted
L64:     removing 3 old packs
L65:     [0:00] 100.00%  3 / 3 files deleted
L66:     done
L67: Afterwards the repository is smaller.
L68: You can automate this two-step process by using the `--prune` switch to `forget`:
L69: 
L70:     $ restic forget --keep-last 1 --prune
L71:     snapshots for host mopped, directories /home/user/work:
L72: 
L73:     keep 1 snapshots:
L74:     ID        Date                 Host        Tags        Directory
L75:     ----------------------------------------------------------------------
L76:     4bba301e  2017-02-21 10:49:18  mopped                  /home/user/work
L77: 
L78:     remove 1 snapshots:
L79:     ID        Date                 Host        Tags        Directory
L80:     ----------------------------------------------------------------------
L81:     8c02b94b  2017-02-21 10:48:33  mopped                  /home/user/work

L108: ## Removing snapshots according to a policy【3†】
L109: 
L110: Removing snapshots manually is tedious and error-prone, therefore restic allows specifying a policy (one or more `--keep-*` options) for which snapshots to keep. You can for example define how many hourly, daily, weekly, monthly and yearly snapshots to keep, and any other snapshots will be removed.
L111: 
L112: Warning
L113: If you use an append-only repository with policy-based snapshot removal, some security considerations are important. Please refer to the section below for more information.
L114: 
L115: Note
L116: 
L117: You can always use the `--dry-run` option of the `forget` command, which instructs restic to not remove anything but instead just print what actions would be performed.
L118: 
L119: The `forget` command accepts the following policy options:
L120: 
L121:   * `--keep-last n` keep the `n` last (most recent) snapshots.
L122:   * `--keep-hourly n` for the last `n` hours which have one or more snapshots, keep only the most recent one for each hour.
L123: 
L124:   * `--keep-daily n` for the last `n` days which have one or more snapshots, keep only the most recent one for each day.
L125: 
L126:   * `--keep-weekly n` for the last `n` weeks which have one or more snapshots, keep only the most recent one for each week.
L127: 
L128:   * `--keep-monthly n` for the last `n` months which have one or more snapshots, keep only the most recent one for each month.
L129:   * `--keep-yearly n` for the last `n` years which have one or more snapshots, keep only the most recent one for each year.
L130:   * `--keep-tag` keep snapshots that match at least one tag list. Each use of the option defines one list: tags separated by commas mean the snapshot must have all of those tags (AND within the list). When `--keep-tag` is given multiple times, the lists are combined with OR (the snapshot is kept if it matches any list). The `forget` command will exit with an error if all snapshots in a snapshot group would be removed as none of them satisfy the tag policy.
L131:   * `--keep-within duration` keep all snapshots having a timestamp within the specified duration of the latest snapshot, where `duration` is a number of years, months, days, and hours. E.g. `2y5m7d3h` will keep all snapshots made in the two years, five months, seven days and three hours before the latest (most recent) snapshot.
